chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Khas'ami from some of his companions from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding the one who was ignorant
and did not stand at al-Muzdalifah and did not spend the night there until he went to Mina, he said: 'He returns.' I said: 'Indeed, that has been missed by him.' He said: 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.الْمُزْدَلِفَة: Muzdalifah, a plain near Mecca where pilgrims gather after standing at Arafat
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (indicating validity despite the omission)
key_terms.مِنًى: Mina, a valley and campsite near Mecca used during Hajj
key_terms.يَرْجِعُ: He returns (implies returning to Muzdalifah to fulfill the obligation)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who misses staying at Muzdalifah due to ignorance?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the night stay at Muzdalifah is a pillar (*rukn*) but its omission due to ignorance (*jahil*) incurs no penalty, distinguishing it from obligatory acts where ignorance might still require compensation. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the validity of Hajj is not contingent upon perfect knowledge of every ritual detail, provided the pilgrim performs the essential rites. The Imam’s concise verdict highlights the ease (*yusr*) intended in Islamic law for those who err in good faith.
